edges.effect_quant: The Cochrane review of 59 studies and 13,342 participants found the largest benefit immediately after treatment (SMD 0.79, 95% CI 0.48-1.09), with smaller short-term (SMD 0.17, 95% CI 0.09-0.26) and medium-term (SMD 0.15, 95% CI 0.04-0.25) effects and no clear long-term advantage.
edges.population: adolescents and adults receiving substance use counseling or brief intervention
edges.mechanism: Motivational interviewing works by lowering resistance to change rather than prescribing a fixed behavioral script. That collaborative style can increase readiness, self-efficacy, and follow-through around reducing alcohol or drug use, but the effect tends to fade when the interviewing dose is brief and no longer reinforced.
edges.summary: The strongest anchor is the Cochrane meta-analysis, which found that motivational interviewing does reduce substance use, but mostly in the near term rather than as a durable long-run fix. Later randomized trials fit that shape: alcohol outcomes often improve, cannabis effects are weaker, and the biggest gains show up when motivation is still fresh after the intervention.
edges.caveats: This edge blends alcohol and drug outcomes across different clinical settings, so the pooled benefit is not equally strong for every substance. The long-term signal is also weaker than the post-intervention signal, which means motivational interviewing often needs reinforcement or follow-on treatment rather than being treated as a one-session cure.

evidence.citation: Smedslund G et al 2011 Cochrane Database Syst Rev
Feldstein Ewing S et al 2022 Exp Clin Psychopharmacol
evidence.notes: Randomized controlled trial of motivational interviewing for alcohol and cannabis use within a predominantly Hispanic adolescent sample.
